Brostek was selected in the first round of the [[1990 NFL draft]] by the Los Angeles Rams with the 23rd overall pick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1990 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1990/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-24 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Brostek played [[Center (American football)|center]] and [[Guard (American football)|guard]] for the Rams throughout his career. After playing left guard for part of 1991, he replaced [[Doug Smith (offensive lineman)|Doug Smith]] as the starting center for the Rams in 1992. Brostek did not miss a [[Down (American football)|down]] during the [[1992 Los Angeles Rams season|1992 season]]. He remained the starting center up to the [[1996 St. Louis Rams season|1996 season]]. Brostek [[Starting lineup|started]] every game for the Rams in 4 seasons (1992,1993,1995,1996), including a string of 35 consecutive starts, but, in his final year (1997), he played only a single game. On October 9, 1997, Brostek was placed on the [[injured reserve]] list for back problems, and his career ended. In that 1992–1997 span, the Rams never had a winning season, though Brostek [[Blocking (American football)|blocked]] for 1,000-yard rushers such as [[Cleveland Gary]] and [[Jerome Bettis]]. In 1997, the Rams finished in last place in the [[NFC West]] division with a won-lost record of 5–11, and he was replaced at starting center by [[Mike Gruttadauria]].

Some of Brostek's teammates included [[Jackie Slater]], [[Keith Loneker]], [[Jim Everett]], [[Henry Ellard]], [[Flipper Anderson]], [[Lawrence Phillips]], [[Tony Banks (American football)|Tony Banks]], [[Chris Miller (quarterback)|Chris Miller]], [[Sean Landeta]], and [[Isaac Bruce]].

==Personal life==
Brostek is currently a [[high school football]] [[Coach (sport)|coach]] at [[Hawaii Preparatory Academy]] in Hawaii. One of Brostek's former players, [[Max Unger]] played football for the [[New Orleans Saints]] after being part of a trade that sent [[Jimmy Graham]] to the [[Seattle Seahawks]], and his son, Shane Brostek, committed to the [[University of Washington]] on a football scholarship.

'''Bennie Lee Cunningham Jr.''' (December 23, 1954 – April 23, 2018<ref name="d650">{{cite web | last=Connolly | first=Matt | title=Former Clemson, Steelers great Bennie Cunningham dies from cancer | website=The State | date=2018-04-23 | url=https://www.thestate.com/sports/college/acc/clemson-university/article209614319.html | access-date=2025-02-05}}</ref>) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[tight end]] for the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was born to Bennie Lee Cunningham Sr., and Carol Cunningham. He was selected out of [[Clemson University]] in the [[1976 NFL draft]] by the Steelers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bennie Cunningham Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/C/CunnBe00.htm |access-date=February 24, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> During his career, he played in 118 games and caught 202 receptions for 2,879 yards and 20 touchdowns.

Cunningham's most famous play in the NFL was a game-winning touchdown in a Pittsburgh home game versus divisional rival Cleveland on September 24, 1978.  It came on a flea-flicker play, culminating in a pass from Terry Bradshaw to Cunningham, who caught the ball in the back right corner of the end zone.  It gave the Steelers a dramatic 15–9 victory over the Browns in sudden-death overtime.

On April 23, 2018, Cunningham died at age 63 at the [[Cleveland Clinic]] in Ohio, where he had been fighting cancer for about three months.

[[Contra Costa College|Contra Costa (JC)]] | undraftedyear = 1972 | pastteams = * [[Dallas Cowboys]] ({{NFL Year|1972}}–{{NFL Year|1982}}) * [[Oakland Invaders|Oakland Invaders (USFL)]] ({{USFL Year|1984}})* | highlights = * [[Super Bowl champion]] ([[Super Bowl XII|XII]]) * [[Stanford Cardinal football|Stanford]] All-Century Team | statlabel1 = Games played | statvalue1 = 138 | statlabel2 = Games started | statvalue2 = 78 | statlabel3 = [[Interceptions]] | statvalue3 = 11 | statlabel4 = [[Fumble|Fumble recoveries]] | statvalue4 = 10 | pfr = BarnBe20 }} '''Benny Jewell Barnes''' (born March 3, 1951) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] for eleven seasons, all with the [[Dallas Cowboys]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Stanford Cardinals football|Stanford Cardinals]] in the [[Pac-12 Conference|Pacific-8 Conference]]. ==Early life== After attending [[John F. Kennedy High School (Richmond, California)|John F. Kennedy High School]] in [[Richmond, California]], he moved on to [[Contra Costa College]] in nearby [[San Pablo, California|San Pablo]], where he was an all-conference [[linebacker]] for the [[American football|football]] team and also an all-conference [[track and field]] athlete. In [[1970 Stanford Indians football team|1970]], Barnes transferred across [[San Francisco Bay|the Bay]] to Stanford, where he was converted from [[linebacker]] to [[free safety]]. He was a two-year starter (24 consecutive starts) and a part of the “Thunder Chickens” defense, that was very effective (9 of the 11 starters played professional football). In [[1971 Stanford Indians football team|1971]], Barnes posted seven interceptions (three against [[Sonny Sixkiller]] at the [[1971 Washington Huskies football team|University of Washington]]){{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=PixOAAAAIBAJ&sjid=v-wDAAAAIBAJ&pg=7085%2C3830090 |work=Spokesman-Review |location=Spokane, Washington |agency=Associated Press |title=Stanford beats UW by 17–6 |date=October 10, 1971 |page=1, sports}}{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=AKFWAAAAIBAJ&sjid=3ecDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6529%2C2011324 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |agency=wire services |title=Stanford knocks off Huskies |date=October 10, 1971 |page=4B}} and was an honorable-mention (second-team) All-Pac-8 selection as a senior.{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=8dlVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=7uADAAAAIBAJ&pg=2574%2C6611603 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |title=Four Ducks on Pac-8 squad |date=November 28, 1971 |page=1B}}{{cite news| title=Bobby Moore again named To All-Pac-8 | newspaper=Santa Cruz Sentinel | date=November 28, 1971| page=18|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/2523758/1971_allpac8_football_team/}} He contributed to teams led by quarterbacks [[Jim Plunkett]] and [[Don Bunce]] in two of the biggest upset victories ever in the [[Rose Bowl Game|Rose Bowl]], in January [[1971 Rose Bowl|1971]] and [[1972 Rose Bowl|1972]], respectively. Although he played just two years, Barnes was inducted into the Stanford Athletic Hall of Fame and selected to the Stanford's All-Century Team. In 2011, he was inducted into the California Community College Athletic Association Hall of Fame. ==Professional career== ===Dallas Cowboys=== In [[1972 Dallas Cowboys season|1972]], he was signed as an [[undrafted free agent]] by the [[Super Bowl]] champion [[Dallas Cowboys]], and made the team based on his excellent [[special teams]] play on [[Punt (gridiron football)|punt]] and [[Kickoff (American football)|kickoff]] coverage. In [[1974 Dallas Cowboys season|1974]], he was named the [[special teams]] captain and by the end of the season he was a starter at left [[cornerback]], but fractured his right ankle and foot against the [[1974 Cleveland Browns|Cleveland Browns]], an injury that would affect him the rest of his career (three surgeries). The next year, he was used on passing downs as the fifth or sixth [[defensive back]] and started 3 games. In [[1976 Dallas Cowboys season|1976]], he regained the starter position at left cornerback in the fifth game after [[Mark Washington (cornerback)|Mark Washington]] suffered 2 concussions at the beginning of the season. Although he didn't have great athletic ability, he compensated with technique, instincts and effort, which made him and underrated part of the team. In [[1977 Dallas Cowboys season|1977]], he was the starter for the [[Super Bowl XII]] winning team. His best season came in [[1978 Dallas Cowboys season|1978]], although he missed three games with ankle and foot problems, he led the team with 5 [[interception]]s, while still excelling on [[special teams]]. In [[Super Bowl XIII]] he was involved in one of the most controversial calls in [[Super Bowl]] history, when [[Lynn Swann]] ran up his back and both fell, resulting in a [[pass interference]] that gave the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] the ball deep in Cowboys territory and an eventual crucial [[touchdown]]. [[NFL Commissioner]] [[Pete Rozelle]], would later concede that the official call was wrong.{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1356&dat=19880824&id=cMVOAAAAIBAJ&sjid=ww4EAAAAIBAJ&pg=5030,1918845 | title=Super Bowl Call on Barnes was Wrong, Rozelle Says | access-date=February 19, 2023}} In [[1979 Dallas Cowboys season|1979]], despite a sore right foot that affected him since [[1975 Dallas Cowboys season|1975]], he tied for the team lead in interceptions and fumble recoveries (including one returned for a 33-yard [[touchdown]]). In the offseason he underwent a joint fusion surgery on his chronically sore right foot. In [[1980 Dallas Cowboys season|1980]], he missed the first five games after having an [[appendectomy]] in the morning of the season opener. The Cowboys went 12–4 in the regular season with Barnes (6 games) and [[Steve Wilson (defensive back)|Steve Wilson]] (10 games) sharing the left [[cornerback]] position. The [[1981 Dallas Cowboys season|next season]], Barnes was moved to [[strong safety]], to improve the depth after the retirement of [[Charlie Waters]] and to make room for [[undrafted free agent]] [[Everson Walls]]. He played as a third-down specialist and had a 72-yard fumble return for a [[touchdown]] in October at [[1981 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco]].{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=eLRQAAAAIBAJ&sjid=VOIDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6799%2C3216325 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |agency=wire services |title=Cowboys fogged in in San Francisco |date=October 12, 1981 |page=3B}} Barnes was waived in August [[1983 Dallas Cowboys season|1983]] at the end of training camp, and replaced with [[undrafted free agent]] [[Bill Bates]].{{cite news| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=861&dat=19830828&id=ErNjAAAAIBAJ&sjid=P4EMAAAAIBAJ&pg=2840,7495062 |work=Victoria Advocate |location=Texas |agency=Associated Press |title=Barnes cut by Cowboys |date=August 28, 1983 |page=1B}} ===Oakland Invaders (USFL)=== On January 14, [[1984 USFL season|1984]], he signed with the [[Oakland Invaders]] of the [[USFL]], reuniting with [[John Ralston (American football)|John Ralston]], his former head coach at Stanford,{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=jVweAAAAIBAJ&sjid=sscEAAAAIBAJ&pg=2644%2C2982519 |work=Times-Daily |location=Florence, Alabama |title=Benny Barnes signs with Oakland Invaders |date=January 15, 1984 |page=2C}} but was released before the season started.{{cite news| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=GLMjAAAAIBAJ&sjid=nyQEAAAAIBAJ&pg=4552%2C6468029 |work=Times-News |location=Hendersonville, North Carolina |agency=Associated Press |title=USFL teams trim rosters; Wranglers sign No.1 choice |date=February 21, 1984 |page=13}} Barnes retired after an 11-year NFL career, where he was part of eight [[NFC Championship Game]]s and three [[Super Bowl]]s. He is considered to be one of the best [[special teams]] players in Dallas Cowboys history. ==Personal life== Barnes spent some time investing in restaurants and worked at Contra Costa College as equipment manager.{{cite web| url=http://nflretirees.blogspot.com/2006/08/for-former-football-pro-its-all-about.html | title=For former football pro, it's all about the students | access-date=February 19, 2023}} He is currently married, with three sons and one daughter. ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} ==External links== * [https://www.baltimoresun.com/sports/bs-xpm-2011-05-06-sc-spt-0506-wildcard-20110506-10-story.html Giving back is an easy call for Barnes] * [https://www.cccaasports.org/HOF/2011/barnes_benny?view=bio CCCAA Hall of Fame bio] *{{Footballstats |nfl=2509007 |cfl= |afl= |espn= |cbs= |yahoo= |fox= |si= |pfr=BarnBe20 |dbf= |rotoworld=}} {{Super Bowl XII}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Barnes, Benny}} [[Category:1951 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:John F. '''Benjamin Malone Jr.''' (February 3, 1952 – March 19, 2020) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Arizona State Sun Devils football|Arizona State Sun Devils]] and was selected by the [[Miami Dolphins]] in the second round of the [[1974 NFL draft]]. He also played for the [[Washington Football Team|Washington Redskins]].

== Early life ==
Malone grew up in [[Eloy, Arizona]] and attended [[Santa Cruz Valley Union High School]].

== College career ==
He played [[college football]] at [[Arizona State University|Arizona State]] and was selected in the second round (47th overall) of the [[1974 NFL draft]] by the [[Miami Dolphins]].

At Arizona State in 1971 he ran for 857 yards and 4 TD while averaging 8.2 yards per carry. 1973 he ran for 1,129 yards and 15 TD while averaging 6.4 yards per carry.<ref>{{cite web| url = https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/benny-malone-1.html| title = Benny Malone College Stats {{!}} College Football at Sports-Reference.com}}</ref> He joined the Sun Devil Sports Hall of Fame in 1983.<ref>{{Cite web|title = asu-football-great-art-malone-dies-at-64|url = http://www.foxsports.com/arizona/story/asu-football-great-art-malone-dies-at-64-073112|website = FOX Sports|access-date = 2016-01-16}}</ref>

==Professional career==
===Miami Dolphins===
Malone was selected by the [[Miami Dolphins]] in the second round (47th overall selection) of the [[1974 NFL draft]]. He played for the Dolphins from 1974 to 1977. In his Miami career, Malone carried the ball 503 times totaling 2,129 yards and 16 rushing touchdowns.  His most significant contribution came in the 1974 Divisional Playoff game at the [[Oakland Raiders]]. Playing for the injured [[Mercury Morris]], Malone ran for 83 yards on 14 carries, including a 23-yard touchdown run with 2:08 remaining that appeared to give Miami the win. But the Raiders scored with 26 seconds left. The TD play became known as "[[The Sea of Hands]]" catch.<ref>{{Cite web|title = The Sea of Hands Game|url = http://www.raiders.com/news/article-1/The-Sea-of-Hands-Game/d192e67a-53ee-4424-868c-a458238b74d2|website = www.raiders.com|access-date = 2016-01-16}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title = Miami Dolphins All Time Depth Chart – Running Back #4|url = http://www.thephinsider.com/2012/6/9/3074043/miami-dolphins-all-time-depth-chart-running-back-4|website = The Phinsider|date = 9 June 2012|access-date = 2016-01-16}}</ref>

===Washington Redskins===
Six games into the 1978 season, Malone was traded to the [[Washington Football Team|Washington Redskins]].<ref>{{Cite web|title = Former NFL running back Art Malone dies at 64|date = August 2012|url = http://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2012/07/31/former-nfl-running-back-art-malone-dies-at-64/|access-date = 2016-01-16}}</ref> He played for the Washington Redskins for the 1978 and 1979 seasons.<ref>{{Cite web|title = Benny Malone|url = http://www.nfl.com/player/bennymalone/2520034/profile|website = NFL.com|access-date = 2016-01-16}}</ref>

'''Robert Jerry Williams''' (September 1, 1954 – May 18, 2020), nicknamed "'''Gentle Ben'''", was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1976 to 1985. Williams was the first Black person to play [[college football]] for the [[Ole Miss Rebels football|Ole Miss Rebels]] of the [[University of Mississippi]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ole Miss Alumni Association |url=http://www.olemissalumni.com/parentsandstudents/default.aspx?page_id=87 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111107091838/http://www.olemissalumni.com/parentsandstudents/default.aspx?page_id=87 |archive-date=November 7, 2011 |access-date=August 2, 2013}}</ref>

Nicknamed "Gentle Ben" during his college days, Williams was a three-time [[Southeastern Conference|All-SEC]] selection. He holds the school record for [[Sack (football)|sacks]] in a single season (18) and in a career (37).<ref name="SI">{{cite magazine |last=Jackson |first=Wilton |date=22 Sep 2022 |title=Ole Miss to Retire Number of School's First Black Football Player |url=https://www.si.com/college/2022/09/22/ole-miss-to-retire-number-of-schools-first-black-football-player |access-date=28 Sep 2022 |magazine=Sports Illustrated |publisher= |quote=Ole Miss announced Thursday that it will retire Ben Williams’s No. 74 jersey number when the Rebels face Mississippi State in the annual Egg Bowl on Nov. 24.}}</ref>

He was selected by the [[Buffalo Bills]] in the third round of the [[1976 NFL draft]]. He was named to the [[Pro Bowl]] in 1982.<ref>[https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WillBe00.htm Ben Williams]. pro-football-reference.com</ref> During his ten years with the Bills, he made 45.5 sacks, a franchise record.<ref name="SI" />

Williams is one of at least 345 [[List of NFL players with chronic traumatic encephalopathy|NFL players to be diagnosed after death with chronic traumatic encephalopathy]] (CTE), which is caused by repeated hits to the head.<ref>{{cite news |title=The driving force behind Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) |website=Concussion Legacy Foundation |url=https://concussionfoundation.org/cte-resources/subconcussive-impacts |access-date=July 2, 2023 |archive-date=July 2, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230702123543/https://concussionfoundation.org/cte-resources/subconcussive-impacts |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=Ken Belson and Benjamin Mueller |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/20/sports/football/cte-study-concussions-brain-tackle.html |title=Collective Force of Head Hits, Not Just the Number of Them, Increases Odds of C.T.E. The largest study of chronic traumatic encephalopathy to date found that the cumulative force of head hits absorbed by players in their careers is the best predictor of future brain disease. |work= [[The New York Times]] |date=June 20, 2023 |access-date=July 2, 2023 }}</ref>

Two years after his death at 65, Ole Miss retired his number, 74, making Williams just the [[Ole Miss Rebels football#Retired numbers|fourth person so honored]]. The ceremony took place on November 24, 2022, as Ole Miss played Mississippi State in the Egg Bowl.<ref name="SI" />

'''Evington Bernard Jackson II''' (born May 10, 1980) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] for the [[Washington Redskins]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]].

Jackson also played for the [[Louisville Fire]] and [[Kentucky Horsemen]].

==Early life==
Jackson attended [[St. Xavier High School (Louisville)|St. Xavier High School]] where he was a three-year starter at [[Linebacker]] in [[High school football|football]], as well as a [[Center (basketball)|center]] in [[basketball]]. In football, he was a two-time 4A All-State selection, as well as an All-Region and All-District selection. He also helped lead his team to two state championships in three seasons, with records of 14–1, 10–2 and 12–3, respectively. As a [[Eleventh grade|junior]], he recorded 120 [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]], seven [[Quarterback sack|sacks]], 19 tackles-for-loses, seven forced [[fumble]]s and five tipped passes that resulted in interceptions. As a [[Twelfth grade|senior]], he recorded 119 tackles, and seven sacks. In football, he was a ''[[Parade Magazine|Parade]]'', ''Blue Chip Illustrated'', ''National Recruiting Advisor'', and ''PrepStart All-America'' selection. He also won state titles in [[Discus throw|discus]] and [[Shot put]].

==College career==
Jackson attended the [[University of Tennessee]], where in [[1998 Tennessee Volunteers football team|1998]], his freshman season, the Volunteers won the [[NCAA Division I FBS National Football Championship|national championship]].

As a freshman in 1998, Jackson played in 12 games, and was one of five true freshmen to play that season. He was a member of the [[Special teams]] and also played as reserve Defensive end. He recorded seven tackles with two quarterback pressures, a sack and a pass broken up. As a sophomore in [[1999 Tennessee Volunteers football team|1999]], he played in 12 games, and earned his first career start. He was a member of the Special teams who also played at Defensive end. For the season, he played in every game, including the [[2000 Fiesta Bowl|Fiesta Bowl]], only missed three quarters. For the season, he recorded 19 tackles, a sack, a tackle-for-loss and a pass broken up. In [[2000 NCAA Division I-A football season|2000]] as a junior, he was primarily a Defensive end, who also played Special teams, and he played in 12 games and started two. In the preseason, he was projected to be a starter, but was a backup to starter DeAngelo Lloyd at Left end, until Lloyd suffered a [[head]] injury against [[LSU Tigers football|LSU]], which forced Jackson to start against [[Georgia Bulldogs football|Georgia]]. For the season, he recorded 12 tackles, including four tackles-for-losses, two recovered fumbles and five quarterback hurries. He earned his second start of the season in the [[2001 Cotton Bowl Classic|Cotton Bowl Classic]], a game in which he recorded five tackles, including two for losses. As a senior in [[2001 NCAA Division I-A football season|2001]], he played in 11 games, starting 10, missing one due to suspension for a violation of team rules. Prior to the regular season games against LSU, Jackson worked his way into the [[Starting lineup|starting]] Left end position. His best game of the season came against [[Kentucky Wildcats football|Kentucky]], in which he recorded eight tackles. For his career, he recorded 78 tackles, three fumble recoveries, five sacks and 10 tackles-for-losses.

==Professional career==

===National Football League===
Jackson went unselected in the [[2002 NFL draft]], however on April 25, he was signed by the [[Washington Redskins]] as a [[Undrafted free agent|rookie free agent]].<ref name="Skins">{{Cite web |date=April 25, 2002 |title=Bernard Jackson, DL, Free Agent -Redskins – Undrafted Rookie Free Agents Added |url=http://www.kffl.com/player/7244/nfl/news/bernard-jackson |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121012085745/http://www.kffl.com/player/7244/nfl/news/bernard-jackson |archive-date=October 12, 2012 |access-date=January 25, 2009 |website=KFFL.com}}</ref> However, on September 1, he was released in the team's final cuts.<ref name="Skins" /><ref name="ESPN">{{Cite web |title=Washington Redskins Transactions – 2002 |url=http://sports.espn.go.com/nfl/teams/transactions?team=was&year=2002 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090609203416/http://sports.espn.go.com/nfl/teams/transactions?team=was&year=2002 |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 9, 2009 |access-date=January 25, 2009 |website=[[ESPN.com]] |publisher=[[ESPN]]}}</ref> However, he was signed the next day to the teams' [[practice squad]].<ref name="Skins" /><ref name="ESPN" /> Then, On November 19, he was promoted to the team's active roster<ref name="Skins" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=November 19, 2002 |title=Transactions – Football – National Football League |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/11/19/sports/transactions-987964.html |access-date=January 25, 2009 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> and played in four games and recorded two tackles. However, on September 1, 2003, he was released again during the team's final cuts,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Washington Redskins Transactions – 2003 |url=http://sports.espn.go.com/nfl/teams/transactions?team=was&year=2003 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120714105740/http://sports.espn.go.com/nfl/teams/transactions?team=was&year=2003 |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 14, 2012 |access-date=January 25, 2009 |website=[[ESPN.com]] |publisher=[[ESPN]]}}</ref> after being sidelined for three weeks with a high [[ankle]] sprain.<ref name="Skins" />

===af2===
In [[2008 af2 season|2008]], after being out of football for four years, Jackson joined [[af2]], a professional [[Arena football]] league. He was assigned to the [[Kentucky Horsemen|Lexington Horsemen]]. On April 10, he was placed on the "Refused to Report" list by the Horsemen.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 10, 2008 |title=Transactions Bulletin #105 |url=http://www.af2.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=21044&SPID=1710&DB_OEM_ID=3525&ATCLID=1409089 |access-date=January 25, 2009 |website=af2.com |publisher=[[af2]]}}{{dead link|date=October 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Then on May 5, he was [[Trade (sports)|trade]]d to the [[Louisville Fire]] for Future Considerations.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 2, 2008 |title=Transactions Bulletin #151 |url=http://www.af2.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=21044&SPID=1710&DB_OEM_ID=3525&ATCLID=1456709 |access-date=January 25, 2009 |website=af2.com |publisher=[[af2]]}}{{dead link|date=October 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> As a rookie in af2, he played in nine games, starting eight. He recorded 19.5 [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]], 4.5 [[Quarterback sack|sacks]], six tackles-for-losses, eight Quarterback hurries, one forced [[fumble]] and three blocked [[Field goal (American football)|kicks]].<ref name="2008 StatGuys">{{Cite web |title=AF2 – 2008 Season Louisville Fire |url=http://www.thestatguys.com/AF2/2008/LOU.HTM#igbg.def |access-date=January 25, 2009 |website=TheStatGuys.com}} {{Dead link|date=October 2010|bot=H3llBot}}</ref> He even returned one kickoff for six yards.<ref name="2008 StatGuys" /> On November 1, he was placed on Re-Assignment,<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 1, 2008 |title=Transactions Bulletin #22 – Part 2 |url=http://www.af2.com/ViewArticle.dbml?ATCLID=1617819&DB_OEM_ID=3525 |access-date=January 25, 2009 |website=af2.com |publisher=[[af2]]}}{{dead link|date=October 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> which means that the league would assign him to another team.

On January 22, 2009, he was reassigned to the Horsemen.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 22, 2009 |title=Transactions Bulletin #67 |url=http://www.af2.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=21044&SPID=1710&DB_OEM_ID=3525&ATCLID=3651456 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090130105556/http://www.af2.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=21044&SPID=1710&DB_OEM_ID=3525&ATCLID=3651456 |archive-date=January 30, 2009 |access-date=January 25, 2009 |website=af2.com |publisher=[[af2]]}}</ref> On April 17, he was suspended by the Horsemen.<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 17, 2009 |title=Transaction Bulletion #135 |url=http://www.af2.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=21044&SPID=1710&DB_OEM_ID=3525&ATCLID=3724239 |access-date=April 24, 2009 |website=af2.com |publisher=[[af2]]}}{{dead link|date=October 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

He is head football coach at [[Robert Morris University]], a position he has held since the 2018 season. Clark played professionally as a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) with the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] and [[Seattle Seahawks]]. He played [[college football]] at the [[University of Miami]] in [[Coral Gables, Florida]]. ==Early life and playing career== Clark, a 1985 graduate of [[A. P. Leto High School]] in [[Tampa, Florida]],{{Cite web |title=Bernard Clark - FIU Athletics |url=http://www.fiusports.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID%3D49161%26SPID%3D4780%26DB_OEM_ID%3D11700%26ATCLID%3D560277%26Q_SEASON%3D2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717054615/http://www.fiusports.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=49161&SPID=4780&DB_OEM_ID=11700&ATCLID=560277&Q_SEASON=2007 |archive-date=July 17, 2011 |access-date=November 7, 2007}} played [[middle linebacker]] while at the [[University of Miami]] from 1985 to 1989. He caught his big break in the [[1988 Orange Bowl]] when he replaced a suspended [[George Mira Jr.]], where he had an outstanding game and was voted Orange Bowl MVP. {{NFL predraft | height ft = 6 | height in = 1 3/8 | weight = 250 | dash = 4.99 | ten split = 1.70 | twenty split = 2.92 | shuttle = 4.50 | cone drill = | vertical = 29.5 | broad ft = 8 | broad in = 6 | bench = 16 | arm span = 32 3/8 | hand span = 8 3/4 | wonderlic = | note = All values from [[NFL Combine]]{{Cite web |title=Bernard Clark, Combine Results, OLB - Miami (FL) |url=https://nflcombineresults.com/playerpage.php?i=25332 |access-date=February 4, 2022 |website=nflcombineresults.com}} }} Clark was selected in the third round in the [[1990 NFL draft]] with the 65th overall pick by the [[Cincinnati Bengals]].{{Cite web |title=1990 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1990/draft.htm |access-date=May 24, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20080327012927/http://www.databasefootball.com/draft/draftyear.htm?yr=1990&lg=NFL 1990 NFL Draft on databaseFootball.com]}} He played two seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), from 1990 to 1991 with the Bengals and the [[Seattle Seahawks]], and two with the [[Orlando Predators]] in the [[Arena Football League]].{{Cite web |title=Hampton University Athletics - Coaching Staff |url=http://www.hamptonpirates.com/coaches.aspx?rc%3D141%26path%3Dfootball |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718165202/http://www.hamptonpirates.com/coaches.aspx?rc=141&path=football |archive-date=July 18, 2011 |access-date=February 10, 2010}} ==Coaching career== Clark began his coaching career at [[James Madison University]], coaching defensive ends from 1998 to 1999. He then coached special teams and linebackers for three years (2000–2003) at [[Liberty University]]. In 2004, he became [[defensive coordinator]] for [[Florida International University]] (FIU). In 2006, Clark became the defensive line coach at the [[University of South Florida]] in his hometown of Tampa for one season before returning to FIU as the defensive line coach in 2007. In 2009, he became the defensive coordinator at [[Hampton University]]. In February 2010, Clark left Hampton to join [[Dave Wannstedt]]'s coaching staff as linebackers coach at the [[University of Pittsburgh]]. Tate also played for the [[Cleveland Browns]], [[Minnesota Vikings]], and [[Pittsburgh Steelers]]. ==Early life== Tate attended [[Stephen Decatur High School (Maryland)|Stephen Decatur High School]] until his junior year, where he was a two-sport star in football and track. In 37 career games, Tate rushed 542 times for 5,920 yards and 78 touchdowns, averaging 10.9 yards per carry and 160 yards per game. He also had 210 career receiving yards. Tate also set the Maryland state records for both career yards rushing (5,920) and total career offensive yards (6,123). For his senior performance, he was awarded the Gatorade State Player of the year and was a consensus All-state pick.{{Cite web |url=http://www.auburntigers.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/tate_ben00.html |title=44 Ben Tate|website=Auburn Tigers |access-date=March 20, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161129210440/http://www.auburntigers.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/tate_ben00.html |archive-date=November 29, 2016 |url-status=dead }} Also a standout [[track & field]] athlete, Tate competed as a [[sprint (running)|sprinter]] and was a state-qualifier in the 100 and 200-meter dashes, reaching the Maryland state finals in both events as a freshman while also placing in the top-three as a sophomore.{{Cite web|url=http://www.cantonrep.com/article/20141031/Blogs/141039819|title=Ben Tate hates times like these}} In addition, Tate also recorded a 4.41-second [[40-yard dash]], had a 32-inch [[vertical jump]] and reportedly bench-pressed a maximum of 355 lb (163 kg) and squatted 630 lb (290 kg).{{Cite web |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/recruiting/player-Benjamin-Tate-29232 |title=Benjamin Tate - Yahoo! Sports |access-date=November 17, 2015 |archive-date=November 21, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151121045347/https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/recruiting/player-Benjamin-Tate-29232 |url-status=dead }} Regarded as a four-star recruit by ''[[Rivals.com]]'', Tate was ranked No. 6 nationally among [[running back]]s and the No. 2 player from the state of Maryland. Upon graduation from Snow Hill High School, Tate received scholarship offers from Auburn, Virginia, Penn State, Maryland, and North Carolina before accepting a scholarship to [[Auburn University]].{{cite web | url=https://n.rivals.com/content/prospects/2006/benjamin-tate-13992 | title=Benjamin Tate | publisher=n.rivals.com | accessdate=July 26, 2017}} ==College career== ===Freshman year=== Tate played sparingly behind senior [[Kenny Irons]], and gained 392 yards on 54 carries in 9 games. He received Freshman All-America Honorable Mention from The Sporting News. Ben's best game was a 156-yard performance against Tulane.{{cite web | url=http://www.auburntigers.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/ben_tate_54755.html | title=Ben Tate | publisher=auburntigers.com | accessdate=July 26, 2017 | archive-date=January 16, 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160116053644/http://www.auburntigers.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/ben_tate_54755.html | url-status=dead }} ===Sophomore year=== [[Image:Carl Stewart.jpg|thumb|right|Tate (#44) talks with teammate [[Carl Stewart (American football)|Carl Stewart]] during a 2007 game at Auburn.]] Tate's sophomore season was a strong one, leading the Tigers in rushing (903 yards on 202 carries for a 4.5 yard average) and to a victory over Clemson in the [[Chick-fil-A Bowl]]. ===Junior year=== Heading into his Junior campaign, Tate was named to several preseason All-SEC teams. However, because of new offensive coordinator [[Tony Franklin (coach)|Tony Franklin]] and his spread, pass-first style of offense, Tate's numbers significantly declined. He gained only 664 yards on 159 carries. ===Senior year=== As the feature back in [[Gus Malzahn]]'s spread offense, Tate shined in his final college season. He gained 1,362 yards on 263 carries with 10 touchdowns. His top performance came against Arkansas, rushing for 184 yards and two touchdowns (over 100 yards coming in the third quarter). Tate also earned AP second-team All-SEC honors, as well as being voted both the Team and Offense MVP award. Tate was also a semi-finalist for the [[Doak Walker Award]]. Tate also led Auburn to a victory over Northwestern in the [[Outback Bowl]], rushing for 108 yards and 2 touchdowns in the overtime win. Tate finished at Auburn 5th on the career rushing list, behind Auburn greats [[Bo Jackson]], [[Carnell Williams]], [[James Brooks (running back)|James Brooks]], and [[Joe Cribbs]]. He rushed for 3321 yards on 678 carries, scoring 24 touchdowns. Tate graduated in May 2009 with a degree in criminology. ==Professional career== [[Image:Ben Tate - Houston Texans.jpg|thumb|right|Tate with the [[Houston Texans]] in 2010]] {{nfl predraft | height ft = 5 | height in = 11 | weight = 220 | dash = 4.43 | ten split = 1.49 | twenty split = 2.52 | shuttle = 4.12 | cone drill = 6.91 | vertical = 40.5 | broad ft = 10 | broad in = 4 | bench = 26 | wonderlic = | arm span = 31¼ | hand span = 9 | note = All values from the [[NFL Combine]]{{Citation |url=http://www.nfl.com/combine/profiles/ben-tate?id=497208 |title=Ben Tate Combine Profile at NFL.com |accessdate=April 2, 2010}} }} ===Houston Texans=== Tate was selected in the second round of the [[2010 NFL draft]] by the [[Houston Texans]] with the 58th overall pick.{{Cite web |title=2010 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2010/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-13 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} Most projected Tate to be picked somewhere in the early to middle of the second round, and recognizing his value at pick 58, the Texans aggressively traded up to draft him. This is the only time in team history that the Texans have drafted a running back earlier than the third round. Tate had high expectations to help a Texans running game that was one of the worst in the league the previous season, but during the Texans pre-season opener in 2010, Tate broke his ankle and was placed on [[Injured reserve list#NFL rules|injured reserve]] (IR).{{cite news|last=McClain|first=John|title=Texans rookie Tate to undergo ankle surgery|url=http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/sports/fb/texansfront/7154571.html|accessdate=August 16, 2010|newspaper=[[Houston Chronicle]]|date=August 15, 2010}} Tate returned healthy for the 2011 season, but was initially placed fourth on the depth chart behind 2010 NFL rushing champion [[Arian Foster]], [[Derrick Ward]], and [[Steve Slaton]]. At the conclusion of the preseason, Tate was listed as the opening-day backup to Ward due to a hamstring injury to Foster. In his NFL debut, Tate did not disappoint, rushing for 116 yards and his first NFL touchdown on 24 carries. He followed that performance the following week against the [[Miami Dolphins]] with another 100-yard game, finishing with 103 yards on 23 carries. He finished the 2011 regular season with 942 rushing yards on 175 attempts (a 5.4 yards-per-carry average, third-highest in the NFL) with 4 rushing touchdowns and 98 total receiving yards in 15 games played, two of which he started (Week 3 against the [[New Orleans Saints]], and week 17 against the [[Tennessee Titans]]). Tate ran for 115 yards against the Cleveland Browns in Week 9 while [[Arian Foster]] ran for 124 yards in the same contest, leading the Texans to 261 yards on the ground, a franchise record.{{cite news|title=Foster, Tate top 100 yards in Texans' 30-12 win|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/nfl/gameflash/2011/11/06/4498/index.html|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120716004147/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/nfl/gameflash/2011/11/06/4498/index.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 16, 2012|accessdate=January 2, 2012|newspaper=[[Sports Illustrated]]|date=November 6, 2011}}[http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/nfl/gameflash/2011/11/06/4498_recap.html Browns vs. Texans, SI.com NFL Game Recap] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111230095036/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/nfl/gameflash/2011/11/06/4498_recap.html |date=December 30, 2011 }} November 6, 2011 Tate played in 11 games in the 2012 season, amassing 279 rushing yards on 65 carries, averaging 4.3 yards per carry. While his per-carry average remained formidable, his carries were limited due to a competitive Houston Texans' backfield along with lingering injuries to his hamstring and foot. It was a frustrating season for the young running back, who had been competing with emerging running back Justin Forsett for backup duties to Arian Foster. In 2013, Tate appeared in 14 games with the Texans, making 7 starts, after a season-ending injury to Arian Foster. Tate responded by rushing for 771 yards and 4 touchdowns, 3 of which came in a Week 13 game against the [[New England Patriots]] where he rushed for a season-high 102 yards. After having battled cracked ribs for much of the season, Tate was placed on injured reserve on December 19, 2013, ending his season.[https://web.archive.org/web/20131220064229/http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap2000000300495/article/ben-tate-ribs-placed-on-houston-texans-ir?campaign=Twitter_atl Ben Tate (ribs) sent to Houston Texans' injured reserve] ===Cleveland Browns=== [[File:Ben Tate 2014 Browns training camp (3).jpg|thumb|Tate with the Browns in 2014]] Tate signed with the [[Cleveland Browns]] on March 15, 2014.{{Cite web |last=Ganguli |first=Tania |date=2014-03-15 |title=Browns agree to deal with ex-Texans RB Tate |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/10613133/ben-tate-cleveland-browns-agree-2-year-deal?ex_cid=espnapi_public |access-date=2024-11-29 |website=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press |language=en}} On October 5, 2014, he ran for a career-high 123 yards on 22 carries in a 29–28 win over the Tennessee Titans.{{Cite web |title=Cleveland Browns at Pittsburgh Steelers - September 7th, 2014 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201409070pit.htm |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} Tate was released by the Browns on November 18, 2014. In the weeks leading up to his release, he grew frustrated with the amount of carries he was getting due to the three-back rotation system the Browns had recently employed, giving Tate, [[Isaiah Crowell]] and [[Terrance West]] fairly even playing time at running back.{{cite web | last=Sessler | first=Marc | title=Cleveland Browns waive Ben Tate after 10 games | website=NFL.com | date=2014-11-18 | url=https://www.nfl.com/news/cleveland-browns-waive-ben-tate-after-10-games-0ap3000000430336 | access-date=2024-11-29}} ===Minnesota Vikings=== The [[Minnesota Vikings]] were awarded Tate on waivers after his release from Cleveland.{{cite web |url=http://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2014/11/19/vikings-claim-ben-tate-off-waivers-after-he-was-cut-by-browns/related/ |title=Vikings claim Ben Tate off waivers after he was cut by Browns |work=[[Pro Football Talk]] |date=November 19, 2014 |access-date=November 19, 2014 |archive-date=November 21, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141121181008/http://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2014/11/19/vikings-claim-ben-tate-off-waivers-after-he-was-cut-by-browns/related/ |url-status=dead }} However, after playing only three games with the team, accumulating 38 rushing yards off of 13 attempts, the Vikings released Tate on December 25, 2014.{{cite web |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/ben-tate-released-by-minnesota-vikings-0ap3000000448804 |title=Ben Tate released by Minnesota Vikings |work=[[NFL Enterprise]] |date=December 23, 2014}} ===Pittsburgh Steelers=== In the lead up to the [[2014 NFL playoffs]], the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] lost [[Le'Veon Bell]] to injury. With no experienced running backs, they signed the newly released Tate on December 30, 2014. In the Wild Card loss against the [[Baltimore Ravens]], Tate had five carries for 19 yards.{{Cite web |title=Wild Card - Baltimore Ravens at Pittsburgh Steelers - January 3rd, 2015 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201501030pit.htm |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} ===The Spring League=== Tate participated in [[The Spring League]] in 2017.{{cite web | url=https://www.profootballrumors.com/2017/04/the-spring-league-announces-training-camp-roster | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170726034951/https://www.profootballrumors.com/2017/04/the-spring-league-announces-training-camp-roster | url-status=dead | archive-date=July 26, 2017 | title=The Spring League Announces Camp Roster | publisher=profootballrumors.com | date=April 9, 2017 | accessdate=July 25, 2017 | author=Levine, Ben}} ==Career statistics== ===NFL=== {| class=wikitable style="text-align:center;" ! rowspan=2|Season !! rowspan=2|Team !! colspan=6|Rushing !! colspan=6|Receiving !! colspan=2|Fumbles |- ! '''BenJarvus Jeremy Green-Ellis''' (born July 2, 1985) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[New England Patriots]] and [[Cincinnati Bengals]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Indiana Hoosiers football|Indiana Hoosiers]] and [[Ole Miss Rebels football|Ole Miss Rebels]]. Green-Ellis was signed by the Patriots as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2008.

Because of his segmented name, Green-Ellis is nicknamed "'''the Law Firm'''". He never had a [[fumble]] with the Patriots.<ref>{{Cite web |last=MacPherson |first=Brian |date=February 4, 2012 |title=After four years without fumbling, Green-Ellis has "ultimate" trust of Patriots coaches |url=http://blogs.providencejournal.com/sports/patriots/2012/02/after-four-years-without-fumbling-green-ellis-has-ultimate-trust.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130201054345/http://blogs.providencejournal.com/sports/patriots/2012/02/after-four-years-without-fumbling-green-ellis-has-ultimate-trust.html |archive-date=February 1, 2013 |access-date=August 21, 2012 |website=[[The Providence Journal]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Graziano |first=Dan |date=September 23, 2012 |title=Rapid Reaction: Bengals 38, Redskins 31 |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/nflnation/post/_/id/63750/rapid-reaction-bengals-38-redskins-31 |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life==
Green-Ellis was born in [[New Orleans|New Orleans, Louisiana]] to Latonia Green and [[Ronald "Slim" Williams|Ronald Ellis]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shaughnessy |first=Dan |date=November 10, 2008 |title=Green-Ellis now the name of the game |url=http://archive.boston.com/sports/football/patriots/articles/2008/11/10/green_ellis_now_the_name_of_the_game/ |access-date=November 10, 2008 |website=Boston.com}}</ref> He attended [[St. Augustine High School (New Orleans)|St. Augustine High School]] in New Orleans, and was a student and a [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in [[High school football|football]] and [[Track and field|track]] for the Purple Knights athletic teams. He was named as an All-City selection and as an All-Metro selection, and the ''[[Clarion Herald]]'' and the ''[[New Orleans Times-Picayune]]'' named him as an All-District selection. Also a standout track athlete, he lettered twice in [[track & field]], where he was an All-District selection and an All-Region selection.

==College career==
Before transferring to Mississippi,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wilson |first=Doug |date=January 27, 2005 |title=Green-Ellis leaving Indiana for Ole Miss |url=https://www.heraldtimesonline.com/story/news/2005/01/27/green-ellis-leaving-indiana-for-ole-miss/48303063/ |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=The Herald-Times |language=en-US}}</ref> Green-Ellis was a productive running back for [[Indiana Hoosiers football|Indiana University]] in the 2003 and 2004 seasons.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 26, 2005 |title=Green-Ellis Leaves Team |url=https://iuhoosiers.com/news/2005/1/26/Green_Ellis_Leaves_Team |access-date=2024-05-15 |website=Indiana University Athletics |language=en}}</ref> Green-Ellis transferred when then-coach [[Gerry DiNardo]] was fired and replaced by [[Terry Hoeppner]] before the 2005 season. As a freshman in 2003, Green-Ellis had a breakout year with 938 yards and seven touchdowns on 225 carries.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BenJarvus Green-Ellis 2003 Game Log |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/benjarvus-green-ellis-1/gamelog/2003 |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> As a sophomore in 2004, Green-Ellis was a part of a two running back rotation with [[Chris Taylor (running back)|Chris Taylor]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2004 Indiana Hoosiers Stats |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/indiana/2004.html |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> Still, he led the team with 794 yards rushing on 231 carries and scored five touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BenJarvus Green-Ellis 2004 Game Log |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/benjarvus-green-ellis-1/gamelog/2004 |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

At [[Ole Miss Rebels football|Ole Miss]], Green-Ellis was only the second running back in the school's history to record back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Borges |first=Ron |date=September 7, 2011 |title=Not easy being BenJarvus Green-Ellis |url=https://www.bostonherald.com/2011/09/07/not-easy-being-benjarvus-green-ellis/ |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=Boston Herald |language=en-US}}</ref> As a junior in 2006, Green-Ellis posted 1,000 yards and seven touchdowns on a school record of 234 carries.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BenJarvus Green-Ellis 2006 Game Log |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/benjarvus-green-ellis-1/gamelog/2006 |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> During his senior season in 2007, he recorded 1,137 yards and six touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BenJarvus Green-Ellis 2007 Game Log |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/benjarvus-green-ellis-1/gamelog/2007 |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He was named as an [[List of All-SEC football teams|All-SEC]] first-team selection by the [[Associated Press]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 5, 2006 |title=2006 Associated Press All-SEC football team|agency=Associated Press |url=https://www.espn.com/espn/wire?section=ncf&id=2686391 |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref>

===New England Patriots===

====2008 season====
Green-Ellis was signed by the Patriots as an undrafted free agent on May 1, 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dunne |first=Tyler |date=January 30, 2012 |title=Super Bowl's undrafted players no longer overlooked |url=http://www.jsonline.com/sports/packers/doing-it-their-way-8m40eaj-138373269.html |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=JSOnline.com |language=en}}</ref> He was waived by the team on August 30, 2008, and signed to the team's practice squad on September 1, 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Battista |first=Judy |author-link=Judy Battista |date=November 11, 2008 |title=Patriots Lose Stars but Get Job Done |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/11/11/sports/football/11patriots.html |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=New York Times |language=en}}</ref> He was promoted to the active roster on October 11.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 11, 2008 |title=Patriots sign RB BenJarvus Green-Ellis to active roster |url=https://www.patriots.com/news/patriots-sign-rb-benjarvus-green-ellis-to-active-roster-154651 |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=Patriots.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

Green-Ellis made his [[National Football League|NFL]] debut on October 12, 2008, recording one catch for nine yards against the [[2008 San Diego Chargers season|San Diego Chargers]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=New England Patriots at San Diego Chargers - October 12th, 2008 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200810120sdg.htm |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> October 20, 2008, the same day that the Patriots placed fellow running back [[Laurence Maroney]] on injured reserve, Green-Ellis had his first NFL start in the Patriots' [[2008 New England Patriots season#Week 7: vs. Denver Broncos|41–7 victory]] against the [[2008 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]] on [[Monday Night Football]]. Green-Ellis had 65 yards on 13 rushes in the second half, and scored his first touchdown on a 1-yard run, entering the end zone untouched.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Denver Broncos at New England Patriots - October 20th, 2008 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200810200nwe.htm |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.projo.com/patriots/content/projo_20081021_green_ellis.133e7edf2.html|title=Green-Ellis has a productive debut in Patriots backfield|work=[[The Providence Journal]]|first=Robert|last=Lee|date=October 21, 2008|access-date=November 17, 2008| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081024080546/http://www.projo.com/patriots/content/projo_20081021_green_ellis.133e7edf2.html| archive-date= October 24, 2008 | url-status= live}}</ref> During [[NBC Sunday Night Football|Sunday Night Football]]'s November 2, 2008, broadcast, [[Al Michaels]] and [[John Madden]] noted that his Patriots teammates had nicknamed Green-Ellis "Law Firm," on account of his multi-part name.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Powell |first=Brian |date=November 3, 2008 |title=SNF Live-Blog: Patriots @ Colts, 1st Half |url=https://awfulannouncing.com/2008-articles/snf-live-blog-patriots-colts-1st-half.html |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=Awful Announcing |language=en-US}}</ref>
[[File:BenJarvus-Green-Ellis 8-28-09 Patriots-vs-Redskins.jpg|thumb|left|"The Law Firm" in his second season with the Patriots]]
In Week 10, against the [[2008 Buffalo Bills season|Buffalo Bills]], Green-Ellis had his first 100-yard game in the NFL (with 105 yards), and scored a touchdown for the fourth consecutive game, giving him a touchdown in every NFL game he had started at the time.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Buffalo Bills at New England Patriots - November 9th, 2008 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200811090nwe.htm |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=BenJarvus Green-Ellis 2008 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GreeBe00/gamelog/2008/ |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> The one-yard touchdown run capped a 92-yard drive whose 19 plays tied a franchise record for most plays on one drive.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.patriots.com/news/index.cfm?ac=latestnewsdetail&pid=35042&pcid=47|title=Patriots vs. Bills game notes|work=[[New England Patriots]]|date=November 9, 2008|access-date=August 10, 2009|archive-date=December 18, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111218092943/http://www.patriots.com/news/index.cfm?ac=latestnewsdetail&pid=35042&pcid=47|url-status=dead}}</ref>

====2009 season====
Green-Ellis played in 12 games in the 2009 season. He had 26 carries for 114 rushing yards.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BenJarvus Green-Ellis 2009 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GreeBe00/gamelog/2009/ |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

====2010 season====

Following the team's trade of Laurence Maroney and early-season injuries to [[Fred Taylor (running back)|Fred Taylor]] and [[Kevin Faulk]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Reiss |first=Mike |date=September 14, 2010 |title=Patriots trade running back Maroney to Denver |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=5572724 |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=September 29, 2010 |title=Patriots Getting Thin at Running Back As Fred Taylor Misses Practice With Toe Injury |url=https://nesn.com/2010/09/patriots-getting-thin-at-running-back-as-fred-taylor-misses-practice-with-toe-injury/ |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=NESN.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Green-Ellis saw an increased role in the Patriots offense. In Week 3, he rushed for 98 yards on 16 carries (6.1 yard average) and a touchdown in a win over the [[2010 Buffalo Bills season|Buffalo Bills]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Buffalo Bills at New England Patriots - September 26th, 2010 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201009260nwe.htm |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He made his first start of the season the next week, rushing for 76 yards on 16 carries and adding another touchdown against the [[2010 Miami Dolphins season|Miami Dolphins]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=New England Patriots at Miami Dolphins - October 4th, 2010 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201010040mia.htm |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> In Week 8, against the [[2010 Minnesota Vikings season|Minnesota Vikings]], he had 17 carries for 112 yards and two touchdowns in the 28–18 victory.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Minnesota Vikings at New England Patriots - October 31st, 2010 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201010310nwe.htm |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> On [[NFL on Thanksgiving Day|Thanksgiving]], Week 12, against the [[2010 Detroit Lions season|Detroit Lions]], Green-Ellis ran for two touchdowns in a Patriots win.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New England Patriots at Detroit Lions - November 25th, 2010 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201011250det.htm |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He added another two touchdowns in a 45–3 Patriots win over the [[2010 New York Jets season|New York Jets]] on ''[[Monday Night Football]]'' in Week 13.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New York Jets at New England Patriots - December 6th, 2010 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201012060nwe.htm |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> In Week 17 against the Dolphins, Green-Ellis eclipsed the 1,000-yard rushing plateau on the season, becoming the first Patriots running back to rush for 1,000 yards since [[Corey Dillon]] in [[2004 New England Patriots season|2004]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=New England Patriots Single-Season Rushing Leaders |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/nwe/single-season-rushing.htm |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

Green-Ellis finished the 2010 season with 1,008 rushing yards on 229 carries (4.4 yard average), and 13 rushing touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GreeBe00/gamelog/2010/ |title=BenJarvus Green-Ellis 2010 Game Log |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |access-date=December 7, 2017}}</ref>

====2011 season====
During the 2011 season, Green-Ellis split playing time with several other running backs, primarily [[Danny Woodhead]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2011 New England Patriots Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees, Injury Reports |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/nwe/2011.htm |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> In Week 5, a 30–21 victory over the [[2011 New York Jets season|New York Jets]], he had 27 carries for 136 yards and two touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New York Jets at New England Patriots – October 9th, 2011 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201110090nwe.htm |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> At the end of the 2011 season, Green-Ellis and the Patriots appeared in [[Super Bowl XLVI]]. He started the game and had ten carries for 44 yards and two receptions for 15 yards, but the Patriots lost 21–17 to the [[2011 New York Giants season|New York Giants]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201202050nwe.htm |title=Super Bowl XLVI – New York Giants vs. New England Patriots – February 5th, 2012 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |access-date=December 6, 2017}}</ref> He rushed for 667 yards from 181 attempts with 11 touchdowns for the AFC Champion Patriots, with a yards per carry average of 3.7. He also had nine receptions for 159 yards.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BenJarvus Green-Ellis 2011 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GreeBe00/gamelog/2011/ |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

===Cincinnati Bengals===
On March 21, 2012, Green-Ellis signed a three-year contract with the [[Cincinnati Bengals]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 22, 2012 |title=Green-Ellis signs three-year deal with Bengals|agency=Associated Press |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/7723790/2012-nfl-free-agency-benjarvus-green-ellis-signs-three-year-deal-cincinnati-bengals |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref> On September 23, in a game against [[2012 Washington Redskins season|Washington]], Green-Ellis recorded his first career fumble, ending an impressive record of 589 touches without a fumble.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 27, 2012 |title=Green-Ellis hopes his first career fumble was his last |url=https://www.nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/green-ellis-hopes-his-first-career-fumble-was-his-last |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=NBC Sports |language=en-US}}</ref> In the following game, a 27–10 win against the [[2012 Jacksonville Jaguars season|Jacksonville Jaguars]], Green-Ellis fumbled two more times, but did not have another fumble the rest of the regular season.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cincinnati Bengals at Jacksonville Jaguars – September 30th, 2012 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201209300jax.htm |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He had four games going over 100 rushing yards in a five-game span from Weeks 11–15. Despite playing in only fifteen games, he gained 1,000 rushing yards in a season for the second time in his career.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BenJarvus Green-Ellis 2012 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GreeBe00/gamelog/2012/ |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]]}}</ref>

Green-Ellis was paired with rookie [[Giovani Bernard]] and as a result of Bernard's effectiveness both rushing and receiving, his snaps declined in the 2013 season.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2013 Cincinnati Bengals Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees, Injury Reports |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/cin/2013.htm |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> In the 2013 season, Green-Ellis had 220 carries for 756 rushing yards and seven rushing touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BenJarvus Green-Ellis 2013 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GreeBe00/gamelog/2013/ |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> On August 29, 2014, he was released by the Bengals, who added [[Jeremy Hill]] in the draft.<ref>{{cite web|work=ESPN.com|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/11431868/rb-benjarvus-green-ellis-cut-cincinnati-bengals|title=Bengals cut BenJarvus Green-Ellis|date=August 29, 2014|first=Coley|last=Harvey|access-date=May 1, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Alper |first=Josh |date=August 13, 2015 |title=BenJarvus Green-Ellis says "phone's been ringing," looking for right team |url=https://www.nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/benjarvus-green-ellis-says-phones-been-ringing-looking-for-right-team |access-date=August 8, 2023 |website=NBC Sports |language=en-US}}</ref>

'''Jesse Bennett Perrin''' (October 20, 1959 – February 3, 2017) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Safety (American football position)|safety]] for four seasons with the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Perrin committed suicide at the age of 57 on February 3, 2017.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.al.com/news/huntsville/index.ssf/2017/02/former_alabama_football_player.html|title=Former Alabama football player dies, coroner says|last=Gattis|first=Paul|date=February 3, 2017|website=AL.com|access-date=February 15, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.timesdaily.com/sports/alabama_football/former-alabama-pro-football-player-perrin-dead-at/article_cbbda7ad-9cba-5ed8-a6b5-635822c54731.html|title=Former Alabama, pro football player Perrin dead at 57|last=Clines|first=Keith|date=February 3, 2017|website=Times Daily|access-date=February 15, 2017}}</ref>

'''Bernard Ford''' (born February 27, 1966) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] and [[Houston Oilers]]. He also was a member of the [[London Monarchs]] in the [[World League of American Football]] (WLAF). He played [[college football]] for the [[UCF Knights football|UCF Knights]]. In 2011 he was inducted into the University of Central Florida Knights Hall of Fame.

==Early life==
Ford attended [[Crisp County High School]], where although he was an All-state selection in track and an MVP in football. He didn't receive many scholarship offers because he was considered small to play [[college football]].

He moved on to [[Marion Military Institute]] and transferred at the end of his freshman year to the [[University of Central Florida]]. As a sophomore, he tallied 13 receptions for 305 receiving yards. The next year, he registered 30 receptions for 653 yards and 8 [[touchdown]]s.<ref>{{cite web |date=October 3, 1986 |title=Ford's Turnaround Gets Big Receptions |url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1986/10/03/fords-turnaround-gets-big-receptions/ |access-date=January 25, 2018 |website=Orlando Sentinel}}</ref>

As a senior, including playoffs, he posted a then school record 82 receptions for 1,403 yards with 13 [[touchdown]]s. He also contributed to his team earning a 9-4 record and a trip to the national semifinals of the [[NCAA Division II]] playoffs. Against [[Northwest Missouri State University]], he had 11 receptions for a school-record 208 yards and 4 [[touchdown]]s.

Ford finished his college career with school records for career receptions (111), career receiving yards (2,138), career touchdown receptions (21), career reception average (19.3), single-season reception average (21.8), career 100-yard receiving games (5), single-season receiving yards (1,403), single-season receptions (68), single-game receptions (14), single-game receiving yards (208 yards) and single-game receiving touchdowns (4).<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/2010/07/10/state-player-countdown-no-20-at-ucf-bernard-ford/ | title=State player countdown: No. 20 at UCF, Bernard Ford | date=July 10, 2010 | access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref>

In 2011, he was inducted into the [[University of Central Florida]] Athletics Hall of Fame.

==Professional career==
===Buffalo Bills===
Ford was selected by the [[Buffalo Bills]] in the third round (65th pick overall) of the [[1988 NFL draft]], after having a standout performance at the [[NFL Scouting Combine]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1988 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1988/draft.htm |access-date=2023-09-24 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1988/02/24/fords-fleet-feet-earn-recognition/ | title=Ford's Fleet Feet Earn Recognition | date=February 24, 1988 | access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref> He separated his shoulder during preseason and was placed on the [[injured reserve list]], where he remained for the entire season. He was waived on September 4, [[1989 NFL season|1989]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1734&dat=19890905&id=Lj4eAAAAIBAJ&sjid=7L4EAAAAIBAJ&pg=2905,446257&hl=en | title= Sports Transactions | access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref>

===Dallas Cowboys===
On September 6, [[1989 NFL season|1989]], Ford was signed by the [[Dallas Cowboys]] to the [[practice squad]].<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.tulsaworld.com/news/aikman-dallas-silent-about-saints/article_8dfd6e39-a855-5cb9-b2f9-0608774cb352.html | title= Aikman, Dallas 'Silent' About Saints | date= September 7, 1989 | access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref> In October, he was promoted to the active roster and appeared in 10 games (one start), posting 7 receptions for 78 yards and one [[touchdown]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1989/10/29/cowboys-are-paying-the-price-for-extensive-roster-changes/ | title= Cowboys Are Paying The Price For Extensive Roster Changes | date= October 29, 1989 | access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref>

===Houston Oilers===
In [[1990 NFL season|1990]], the [[Houston Oilers]] signed Ford as a [[Plan B free agency|Plan B free agent]] to play in their [[run and shoot offense]] and return kickoffs.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1990/04/01/ford-plans-for-life-after-professional-football/ | title= Ford Plans For Life After Professional Football | date= April 1990 | access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref> He appeared as a backup in 14 games, recording 10	receptions for 98 yards, one [[touchdown]] and 14 kickoff returns for 219 yards. He wasn't re-signed at the end of the season.

===London Monarchs===
On February 4, [[1992 NFL season|1992]], he was selected by the defending champions the [[London Monarchs]], in the second round of the [[World League of American Football|WLAF Draft]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1992/02/05/thunder-roll-dice-with-rocker-in-wlaf-draft/ | title=Thunder Roll Dice With Rocker In WLAF Draft | date=February 5, 1992 | access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref> He was a starter at [[wide receiver]], registering 45 receptions for 833 yards and 6 [[touchdown]]s.

===Green Bay Packers===
On June 11, [[1992 NFL season|1992]], he signed with the [[Green Bay Packers]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1320&dat=19920613&id=hERWAAAAIBAJ&sjid=guoDAAAAIBAJ&pg=4179,3376617&hl=en | title= Packers Sign Majkowski | access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref> He was released on August 24.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1734&dat=19920825&id=xecbAAAAIBAJ&sjid=31IEAAAAIBAJ&pg=2772,5208040&hl=en | title=Transactions | access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref>

===Miami Dolphins===
On March 3, [[1993 NFL season|1993]], he was signed by the [[Miami Dolphins]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1893&dat=19930303&id=5qofAAAAIBAJ&sjid=AdcEAAAAIBAJ&pg=3446,460252&hl=en | title= Transactions | access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref> He was cut on July 30.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=861&dat=19930731&id=XrMLAAAAIBAJ&sjid=91UDAAAAIBAJ&pg=4557,5765221&hl=en | title= Transactions | access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref>

===Philadelphia Eagles===
In [[1995 NFL season|1995]], he was signed by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]]. He was waived on July 31.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1290&dat=19950801&id=6tQPAAAAIBAJ&sjid=lY4DAAAAIBAJ&pg=4062,62308&hl=en | title=Philadelphia Eagles | access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref>

'''Benjamin "Ben" Guidugli''' (born October 22, 1987) is an American former [[American football|football]] [[Fullback (American football)|fullback]]. He was signed by the [[St. Louis Rams]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2011. He played [[college football]] for the [[University of Cincinnati]].

==Professional career==

===St. Louis Rams===
On July 28, 2011, Guidugli was signed as an undrafted free agent by the [[St. Louis Rams]].<ref name="Giants sign Guidugli 2013">{{cite web |url=http://www.giants.com/news-and-blogs/article-1/FB-Ben-Guidugli-signs-DImperio-retires/21d1c75a-90c9-4c60-aeb7-5e028d4ca152 |title=FB Ben Guidugli signs; D'Imperio retires |last=Eisen |first=Michael |date=August 13, 2013 |website=Giants.com |accessdate=August 14, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130815080200/http://www.giants.com/news-and-blogs/article-1/FB-Ben-Guidugli-signs-DImperio-retires/21d1c75a-90c9-4c60-aeb7-5e028d4ca152 |archive-date=August 15, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===New York Giants===
On August 13, 2013, Guidugli was signed by the [[New York Giants]] to replace [[Fullback (American football)|fullback]] [[Ryan D'Imperio]], who decided to retire from the NFL.<ref name="Giants sign Guidugli 2013"/> On August 25, 2013, he was cut by the Giants.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.giants.com/news-and-blogs/article-1/LB-Aaron-Curry-among-players-released/4c5623fc-f421-491a-a843-0e3cb78cf38c |title=LB Aaron Curry among players released |last=Eisen |first=Michael |date=August 26, 2013 |website=Giants.com |accessdate=September 4, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130829084616/http://www.giants.com/news-and-blogs/article-1/LB-Aaron-Curry-among-players-released/4c5623fc-f421-491a-a843-0e3cb78cf38c |archive-date=August 29, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Personal life==
